about: Jean-Paul Brun’s family estate is in Charnay, in the southern Beaujolais just north of Lyon, in the country of the pierres dorées, the golden, iron-tinted limestone that gives the domaine its name. Brun started with about four hectares and now farms more than sixty. In the mid-2000s he began buying land in the northern crus, and the Côte de Brouilly was his first cru bottling. He is widely credited with keeping old-style Beaujolais alive: wines of fruit and freshness rather than weight.

Côte de Brouilly is the steep hill at the heart of the larger Brouilly cru. Brun’s vines there are 50 to 60 years old, rooted in decomposed volcanic granite on the mid-slope, facing the rising sun. He avoids the commercial yeast most Beaujolais relies on and does not routinely chaptalise. The grapes are destemmed and fermented with native yeasts in concrete, with no sulphur during fermentation and a maceration of three to four weeks. The wine then ages six to eight months in concrete and is lightly filtered, with minimal sulphur, before bottling.

Brun calls 2022 a warm vintage of very soft tannins and supple structure. Tasting it at the domaine in 2024, Bill Nanson of the Burgundy Report found it vibrant with red fruit, deeper than the cuvées before it, and memorable for the depth of its finish. Brun makes his crus to be enjoyed young but with enough structure to age a few years, and this one sits at the more serious end of his range.
facts: Destemmed, native-yeast fermentation in concrete, 3–4 week maceration (not carbonic)
